title: San Francisco Bay Expeditions
subtitle: Sea and land approaches to San Francisco Bay, 1542 to 1776, after the Mission Dolores exhibit panel, with the Manila galleon run that passed them by
abstract: The exploration of the San Francisco and Monterey coast as the Mission Dolores exhibit panel presents it: five sea approaches, Ayala's longboat surveys inside the bay in 1775, and the land expeditions of 1769 to 1776. Every course drawn here is interpretive, a generalized line meaning the party passed roughly this way, traced after the panel and the published diaries, and never a surveyed track. The stops carry the diary account of what happened at each place, and say where the published reconstructions disagree with each other. Links to records in the Archives of California are catalogue-level matches, not leaf-verified.
legend_note: All courses are generalized and interpretive, after the Mission Dolores exhibit panel and the published diaries. Record links are catalogue-level matches.

routes.label: Manila galleons, 1565-1815

stops.name: The Manila ships' landfall run
stops.summary: Returning galleons made their American landfall to the north and ran south along this coast for Acapulco, year after year from 1565 until 1815. Only the first two centuries of that run fall inside the period this map covers, and no galleon ever entered the bay: the line is the traffic that passed the Gate without finding it. Course generalized and interpretive.

routes.label: Drake, 1579

stops.name: Drake careens in 'a faire and good bay'
stops.summary: Five weeks ashore among the Coast Miwok. The quoted phrase is from the narrative Hakluyt printed, which has the ship driven back south from forty-three degrees until 'it pleased God to send us into a faire and good bay, with a good winde to enter the same', and anchoring there on 17 June; its own heading says Drake landed where he found 'a faire and goodly haven'. The World Encompassed, the 1628 account usually cited for the landfall, words it differently: the ship 'fell with a conuenient and fit harborough' in 38 degrees 30 minutes and lay there until 23 July. The landing site is a long-running argument; Drakes Bay is the prevailing identification and the one the exhibit panel follows.
stops.notes: Site identification debated; shown at Drakes Bay per the panel.

routes.label: Ayala & Canizares, 1775

stops.name: The San Carlos enters the bay

date.display: 5 August 1775 (entry); the ship moved to Angel Island later that month

stops.summary: Ayala brought the first ship through the Gate, at night, with the launch sent in ahead of the packet. The San Carlos anchored inside on arrival and only afterwards moved to the island Ayala named for Our Lady of the Angels, where she lay for the rest of a stay of forty-four days while Jose de Canizares surveyed the bay by longboat and Juan Bautista de Aguirre took the southern arm. The land expedition Ayala was waiting for never appeared. The entry is dated 5 August 1775 from the ship's own diaries, published by Galvin in 1971; Bancroft, who had only Palou and no diary or map of the survey, put the entry on the night of 1 August and the move to Angel Island on the 2nd, taking the island's name from that day.

sources.citation: Galvin (ed.), The First Spanish Entry into San Francisco Bay, 1775 (San Francisco: John Howell Books, 1971); after the Mission Dolores exhibit panel.

routes.label: Portola-Crespi-Rivera-Serra, 1769

stops.name: The bay discovered from Sweeney Ridge
stops.summary: The first European sight of San Francisco Bay, and not by the party sent to look for it. On 1 November 1769 Sergeant Ortega went north with a small party and three days' provisions to settle whether Monterey had been passed; while he was away, on 2 November, soldiers from the camp went up these hills after deer and came back with word of a great inland sea reaching north and south-east as far as they could see. Bancroft: the names of the deer hunters can never be known. Ortega returned on the 3rd, unable to cross the inlet, but carrying what he had understood from the people of the peninsula: that at the head of the arm of the sea lay a harbour with a vessel at anchor in it. It was that report, and the hope that the vessel was the San Jose with their supplies, that moved the camp. On 4 November the whole company broke camp, crossed the hills north-eastward and looked down from the summit on the inland sea.

sources.citation: Bancroft, History of California I (San Francisco: The History Company, 1884), 159-60, following Crespi's and Costanso's diaries.

routes.label: Portola's second march to Monterey, 1770

stops.name: Monterey recognized and occupied
stops.summary: Monterey was identified at last and the presidio and mission of San Carlos founded here on 3 June 1770. No probe north followed under Portola: as soon as a beginning had been made he handed the government of the new establishments to Pedro Fages as military commandant and sailed for San Blas in the San Antonio on 9 July 1770, taking the engineer Costanso with him. The order to explore the port of San Francisco was written in Mexico on 12 November 1770 and reached Fages at Monterey in May 1771; he could not act on it until the spring rains of 1772 had passed.

sources.citation: Bancroft, History of California I (San Francisco: The History Company, 1884), 174, 183-84.

routes.label: Fages and Crespi, 20 March to April 1772

stops.name: The Strait of Carquines
stops.summary: Fages left Monterey on 20 March 1772 with Crespi, twelve soldiers, a muleteer and an Indian, under the viceroy's order to find the port of San Francisco. Marching up the eastern bayshore he was stopped here: trying to get round the round bay, which Crespi thought large enough for all the armadas of Spain, the party found the narrows barring the way. They followed the treeless hills along the strait, were received at five large villages whose people came across from the far shore on rafts, and camped on a stream near the shore, probably the Arroyo del Hambre near Martinez.

sources.citation: Bancroft, History of California I (San Francisco: The History Company, 1884), 184-86.

Crespi, Diario que se formo en el registro que se hizo del puerto de Nuestro Serafico Padre San Francisco, printed in Palou, Noticias, i. 481-501; trans. in Crespi's diary, ed. Brown, A Description of Distant Roads.

stops.name: The river mouths from the Willow Pass hills
stops.summary: On 30 March the party left the strait, advanced two leagues to the Arroyo de las Nueces near Pacheco, crossed Mount Diablo Creek and climbed a range of low hills near Willow Pass. From the summit they looked down on the two broad rivers and their channels, sloughs and islands, which Crespi described closely, then crossed four or five leagues of plain to camp half a mile from the bank of the great river, which they named the Rio de San Francisco: the San Joaquin, at or near Antioch. It is the farthest inland any Spanish party had yet seen, and the first European sight of the delta.

sources.citation: Bancroft, History of California I (San Francisco: The History Company, 1884), 186.

routes.label: Rivera and Palou, outbound by the interior, 23 November to 4 December 1774

stops.name: The cross above the Seal Rocks
stops.summary: From the camp on Lake Merced, Rivera took four soldiers and Palou north-west over the dunes to the beach and followed it until a steep hill stopped them, in sight of the pointed rocks offshore. They climbed it, set up a cross on the summit and were back in camp within four hours. This is the marker Ayala's men had missed the summer before and that later parties found still standing. Rivera had set a first cross a week earlier, on 28 November, on San Francisquito Creek, as a sign that San Francisco was to be founded there; Palou came home from the trip with six sites he thought fit for missions, at Hollister, San Francisquito Creek, two vales between Spanish Town and Pescadero, Santa Cruz on the San Lorenzo, and Watsonville on the Pajaro.

routes.label: Rivera and Palou, the coastal return, 5 to 13 December 1774

stops.name: Into the shore trail of 1769
stops.summary: Exploration of the Rio de San Francisco was put off until after the rains and the party turned for home by the shore route of 1769. Three hours south of Lake Merced on 5 December they struck the old trail, crossed the San Lorenzo and the Pajaro on the 11th and reached the presidio of Monterey on 13 December 1774. This coastal line is the leg they travelled last, not the way they came.

routes.label: Anza-Font, 1776

stops.name: The presidio site chosen at the Gate
stops.summary: A table-land commanding the narrows, picked for the presidio on 28 March 1776. Font had written the day before, looking at the port from this side of the water, that it was the harbour of harbours. The white cliff above the Gate became the presidio of San Francisco that autumn.

sources.citation: Font's complete diary, entries of 27 and 28 March 1776, in Bolton, Anza's California Expeditions IV; after the Mission Dolores exhibit panel.

stops.name: The arroyo de los Dolores chosen for the mission
stops.summary: The sheltered creek and lagoon two leagues in from the Gate, named for the Friday of Sorrows: the site of Mission San Francisco de Asis, where these exhibit panels hang today.

sources.citation: After the exhibit panel; Font's complete diary (Bolton IV).

stops.name: To the mouths of the rivers
stops.summary: Anza and Font round the southern bay, run the eastern shore past the strait, and look into the delta before turning for home: the whole future mission-and-presidio geography seen in one circuit.
